1.text_clean:
1. A student attaches one end of a copper wire to an oscillator operating at a fixed frequency. The other end of the wire passes over a pulley to weights that hang vertically. The first harmonic standing wave is established by using the slider to change the length of the wire. The procedure is repeated for different weights.
[Diagram: wire stretched from an oscillator over a slider and a pulley to hanging weights]
The mass $m$ of the weights and the wavelength $\lambda$ of the wave are related by
$m = \frac{\mu f^2}{g}\lambda^2$
where $\mu$ is a constant, $f$ is the frequency of the wave and $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.
(a) Deduce the unit of $\mu$ in terms of fundamental SI units. [1]
(b) The graph shows the data obtained by the student, plotted to show the variation of $m$ with $\lambda^2$.
[Graph: m / g (0 to about 180) against $\lambda^2$ / m$^2$ (0 to 1.0); six data points with vertical error bars from about (0.17, 29) to (0.82, 175)]
(i) Draw the line of best fit for these data. [1]
(ii) Identify the evidence for a systematic error in the data. [1]
(iii) Suggest a possible reason for the systematic error. [1]
(iv) Calculate the gradient of the graph. [2]
(c) The percentage uncertainty of the gradient is 6.0%. The frequency $f$ of the wave is $(60.0 \pm 2.0\%)$ Hz.
Estimate, using the answer to (b)(iv), $\mu$ for the string. Include the percentage uncertainty of $\mu$ in your answer. [2]

2.text_clean:
2. A student wants to verify the relation $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$ between the period $T$ of a simple pendulum and the length $L$ of the pendulum, where $g$ is the acceleration of free fall. The student operates a stopwatch to measure one oscillation and a millimeter ruler to measure the length of the pendulum.
(a) State, for this experiment,
(i) one variable that must be controlled, [1]
(ii) the main source of error in $T$. [1]
(b) To determine $T$ more precisely, the student measures the total time for 20 oscillations and divides by 20.
Suggest why this is preferable to measuring the time for just one oscillation. [2]
(c) (i) The student plots a graph with $L$ on the horizontal axis. State the variable that must be plotted on the vertical axis in order to obtain a line of best fit that is straight. [1]
(ii) Calculations using the data of the experiment show that $g = 9.71622\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ with a percentage uncertainty of 8%. Determine the value of $g$ that can be obtained from this experiment. Include the absolute uncertainty in $g$ to one significant figure. [2]

3.text_clean:
3. A proton is moving in a region of magnetic field of strength $B$. The speed of the proton relative to the magnetic field is $v$.
[Diagram: magnetic field into the page (crosses); proton moving to the right with velocity v]
In the reference frame in which the magnetic field is at rest, the proton experiences an initial magnetic force $evB$ upwards.
(a) Outline why there can be no magnetic force on the proton in the proton's rest frame. [1]
(b) Discuss the nature of the force in the proton's rest frame. [2]
3.note: audit: relativity of magnetic force on moving charge; matches six A.5+D.3 equivalents

4.text_clean:
4. The diagram shows the axes of a coordinate system S at rest relative to the Earth. Earth is at the origin of S.
[Spacetime diagram: ct / ly (0 to 5) against x / ly (0 to 5); ct' axis through (4, 5) and x' axis through (5, 4)]
$x'$ and $ct'$ are the coordinates of a reference frame S' in which a spacecraft is at rest. When the origins of the two sets of axes coincide, all clocks in the frames show zero.
(a) Show that the speed of the spacecraft is $0.80c$ as measured in S. [1]
(b) (i) An event has coordinates $x = 0$ and $ct = 0.60$ ly in S. Show, using a Lorentz transformation, that the time coordinate of this event in S' is $ct' = 1.00$ ly. [2]
(ii) Label, on the diagram with the letter P, the point on the $ct'$ axis whose $ct'$ coordinate is 1.00 ly. [2]
(c) At $ct = 0$, a light beam is sent from Earth to a space station at rest 4.0 ly away in S. Event R is the arrival of the light beam at the space station.
(i) Draw lines to indicate R on the diagram. [2]
(ii) Determine, using the diagram or otherwise, the space coordinate $x'$ of event R in S'. [2]

5.text_clean:
5. A muon is an unstable particle with a half-life of 1.56 μs as measured in the muon's rest frame. Muons are produced in a laboratory and are all directed at a speed $0.866c$ towards a muon detector. The gamma factor ($\gamma$) for this speed is 2.00. The detector, according to observers in the laboratory, is a distance $D$ from the muon source.
[Diagram: muon source and detector separated by distance D]
(a) According to laboratory observers $\frac{\text{number of muons detected}}{\text{number of muons produced}} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Calculate $D$. [2]
(b) In the muon source rest frame (frame S), the detector is approaching at a speed $0.866c$.
In frame S,
(i) show that the distance travelled by the detector when it meets the muon source is 405 m. [1]
(ii) determine the time taken for the detector to reach the muon source. [1]
(c) Calculate, using the answers to (b)(i) and (b)(ii) the ratio $\frac{\text{number of muons detected}}{\text{number of muons produced}}$ in S. [2]
(d) Comment on the ratios in (a) and (c). [2]

6.text_clean:
6. A proton is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 3.40 GV.
(a) Calculate, in GeV $c^{-1}$, the momentum of the proton. [3]
(b) Calculate, in terms of $c$, the speed of the proton. [2]

7.text_clean:
7. A gamma-ray photon of frequency $f_0$ is emitted from the top T of a tower towards the base B of the tower.
[Diagram: tower on Earth; photon travels down from top T to base B]
(a) Explain, by reference to the equivalence principle, why the frequency of the photon measured at B will be larger than $f_0$. [3]
(b) Two identical clocks at T and B use the period of a light wave to measure time intervals. Explain whether observers at T observe the clock at B to be running slower or faster. [2]

8.text_clean:
8. A uniform rod of length 1.20 m is at rest on a horizontal surface. The rod is pivoted at its centre so that it is free to rotate about a vertical axis through the centre.
[Diagram (top view): rod of length 1.20 m pivoted at its centre; particle moving at 12.0 m s$^{-1}$ perpendicular to the rod towards one end]
A particle of mass 0.200 kg moving with speed 12.0 m s$^{-1}$ collides with and sticks to one end of the rod.
(a) The moment of inertia of the rod about the axis is 0.180 kg m$^2$. Show that the moment of inertia of the rod–particle system is about 0.25 kg m$^2$. [1]
(b) Show that the angular speed of the system immediately after the collision is about 5.7 rad s$^{-1}$. [2]
(c) Calculate the energy lost during the collision. [2]
(d) A frictional torque of magnitude 0.152 N m acts on the system just after it begins to rotate. Calculate
(i) the angular deceleration of the rod. [1]
(ii) the number of revolutions made by the rod until it stops rotating. [2]
(e) In another situation the rod rests on a horizontal frictionless surface with no pivot. Predict, without calculation, the motion of the rod–particle system after the collision. [2]

9.text_clean:
9. The $pV$ diagram shows a heat engine cycle consisting of adiabatic, isothermal and isovolumetric parts. The working substance of the engine is an ideal gas.
[pV diagram: cycle A → B (isothermal expansion), B → C (isovolumetric pressure drop), C → A (steeper adiabatic compression)]
The following data are available:
$p_A = 5.00 \times 10^5$ Pa
$V_A = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^3$
$T_A = 602$ K
$p_B = 3.00 \times 10^4$ Pa
$p_C = 4.60 \times 10^3$ Pa
(a) Suggest why AC is the adiabatic part of the cycle. [2]
(b) Show that the volume at C is $3.33 \times 10^{-2}$ m$^3$. [2]
(c) Suggest, for the change A ⇒ B, whether the entropy of the gas is increasing, decreasing or constant. [2]
(d) Calculate the thermal energy (heat) taken out of the gas from B to C. [2]
(e) The highest and lowest temperatures of the gas during the cycle are 602 K and 92 K.
The efficiency of this engine is about 0.6. Outline how these data are consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. [2]

10.text_clean:
10. A sphere floats in water. The sphere is pushed downwards by a small amount and is then released.
[Diagram A: sphere in equilibrium at the water surface; Diagram B: sphere displaced downward]
(a) Draw and label on diagram B the forces acting on the sphere just after it has been released. [1]
(b) After it is released, the sphere performs damped oscillations. The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the amplitude of oscillations $A$.
[Graph: A / cm against t / s (0 to 5 s); damped oscillation with period about 1 s, peaks 2.0, 1.5, 1.1, 0.8, 0.6 cm]
(i) Calculate the $Q$ factor for this system. [2]
(ii) The water is replaced by another liquid of higher viscosity. State and explain the effect of this on the $Q$ factor of the system. [2]

11.text_clean:
11. A siphon consists of a pipe AB of constant diameter that is used to empty a large tank of oil. The depth of the oil in the tank is 5.0 m and the outlet B of the pipe is 8.0 m below the free surface of the oil in the tank.
[Diagram (not to scale): large tank of oil 5.0 m deep; siphon pipe from A in the tank rising a height h above the oil surface then descending to outlet B, 8.0 m below the oil surface]
(a) Show, using Bernoulli's equation, that the speed of the oil as it leaves opening B is 12.5 m s$^{-1}$. [2]
(b) Suggest why the speed of the oil everywhere in the siphon is the same as that at B. [1]
(c) Calculate the maximum height $h$ for which the siphon will work. The density of oil is 915 kg m$^{-3}$ and the atmospheric pressure is $1.01 \times 10^5$ Pa. [2]

12.text_clean:
12. A converging lens is placed between an object and a screen. An image of the object is formed on the screen.
[Diagram (not to scale): upright object, converging lens, inverted image on a screen]
(a) Draw a ray to locate the focal point of the lens. Label this point with the letter F. [1]
(b) The focal length of the lens is 4.0 cm and the height of the image is half the height of the object. Determine the distance of the object from the lens. [3]
(c) The lens suffers from spherical aberration.
(i) Draw lines to complete the rays in the diagram. [1]
[Diagram: lens on a grid with two parallel rays incident, one far from and one close to the principal axis]
(ii) Describe the effect of spherical aberration on the image formed by the lens. [1]
(iii) State how spherical aberration may be corrected. [1]
(d) A simple optical astronomical refracting telescope consists of an objective lens of focal length 75 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4.0 cm. The telescope is used to view the Moon. The Moon subtends an angle of 0.51° at the unaided eye.
(i) Calculate the angle subtended by the Moon when viewed through the telescope. [2]
(ii) The telescope is now turned around so that the eye of the observer is behind the objective lens. State the change, if any, in the image of the Moon. [1]

13.text_clean:
13. A ray of monochromatic light is incident on an optical fibre making an angle of $\theta$ with the normal. The refractive index of the core is 1.500 and the refractive index of the cladding is 1.489.
[Diagram: ray entering the end of an optical fibre from air at angle θ to the normal, refracting into the core and reflecting at the cladding]
(a) (i) Calculate the critical angle $\theta_c$ at the core-cladding boundary. [2]
(ii) Determine the maximum value of $\theta$ such that the ray is incident on the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle. [2]
(b) The diagram shows two rays following different paths in the optical fibre. Ray 1 travels along the axis of the fibre. Ray 2 is incident on the core-cladding boundary at an angle $\varphi$ just greater than $\theta_c$.
[Diagram: ray 1 along the fibre axis; ray 2 zig-zagging by reflection at angle φ]
The length of the optical fibre is 1 km. Show that the time delay between the arrival of the two rays at the end of the optical fibre is about 37 ns. [3]
(c) A signal transmitted by the optical fibre consists of very narrow digital pulses. The pulses are 37 ns apart. The graph shows the variation with time of the amplitude of two consecutive pulses input to the optical fibre.
(i) Sketch, on the axes, the variation with time of the amplitude of the two pulses after they have travelled by all possible ray paths along a 1 km length of the optical fibre. [2]
[Graph: amplitude against time; two narrow rectangular input pulses 37 ns apart; "received" region with dashed lines 37 ns apart]
(ii) State what would happen when the input pulses are separated by less than 37 ns. [1]

14.text_clean:
14. (a) Describe, in the context of medical diagnosis, how an ultrasound A scan is produced. [2]
(b) The diagram shows a simplified view of the front of a human eye.
[Diagram: front of a human eye showing cornea and lens, with a transducer placed at the cornea]
A transducer is placed at the cornea and an ultrasound pulse is emitted.
(i) Draw, on the axes, the expected A scan for just the part of the eye shown. [2]
[Axes: signal strength against time, with the emitted ultrasound pulse shown near the origin]
(ii) Demonstrate how the A scan in (b)(i) can be used to obtain a value for the thickness of the eye lens. [2]
(c) In magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a patient is exposed to a strong external magnetic field and a radio frequency signal (RF) is emitted towards the patient.
(i) Explain the reason for using the RF signal. [2]
(ii) Describe the subsequent measurements that can be used to distinguish between different types of tissues. [2]

15.text_clean: 15. Distinguish between open stellar clusters and globular stellar clusters. [1]

16.text_clean:
16. The graph shows an incomplete Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram. The position of the Sun and three other stars, A, B and C, are shown.
[HR diagram: $L/L_\odot$ against $T$ / $10^3$ K (30.0, 6.0, 3.0); main sequence through the Sun at (6.0, 1); A on the main sequence at 30.0 × 10³ K at the top; B at 3.0 × 10³ K at the same luminosity as A; C at 30.0 × 10³ K below the Sun's luminosity]
$M_\odot$, $R_\odot$ and $L_\odot$ are the mass, radius and luminosity of the Sun.
(a) The mass of star A is $52 M_\odot$. Show that the luminosity of star A is about $10^6 L_\odot$. [1]
(b) Determine the radius of star B in terms of $R_\odot$. [3]
(c) Describe the main stages in the evolution of star A after leaving the main sequence. [3]
(d) The luminosity of star C is $2.4 \times 10^{23}$ W and its apparent brightness is $4.1 \times 10^{-14}$ W m$^{-2}$. Determine the distance, in pc, to star C. [2]
(e) Suggest whether the method of stellar parallax can be used to measure the distance to star C. [1]

17.text_clean:
17. A distant galaxy emits light of wavelength 486 nm. The light received on Earth has wavelength 512 nm.
(a) Determine the recession speed of the galaxy. [2]
(b) Estimate the distance to the galaxy in pc. Take the Hubble constant as 72 km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. [1]
(c) Astrophysicists continue to seek an accurate value of the Hubble constant. State the importance of this constant for cosmology. [1]

18.text_clean:
18. (a) Light from a distant intergalactic cloud shows a redshift of 1.74. Show that the size of the universe when the light was emitted, relative to its present size, is 0.365. [1]
(b) (i) Demonstrate that the temperature of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is proportional to $\frac{1}{R}$ where $R$ is the cosmic scale factor of the universe. [2]
(ii) The temperature of the CMB has been measured by studying carbon absorption lines in the intergalactic cloud in (a). The temperature measured is 7.4 K.
Calculate the present value of the CMB temperature. [2]

19.text_clean:
19. (a) A spherical nebula has radius $9 \times 10^{15}$ m and contains $10^{10}$ atoms of hydrogen per cubic metre. Show that the mass of the nebula is about $5 \times 10^{31}$ kg. [2]
(b) The Jeans mass $M_J$, in kg, for a nebula containing hydrogen at a Kelvin temperature $T$ is given by
$M_J = 1.8 \times 10^{33}\left(\frac{T}{100}\right)^{1.5}$
The nebula in (a) has a temperature of 50 K. Suggest why this nebula will not collapse to form a star. [2]
(c) (i) The temperature of the nebula is decreasing. Estimate the temperature at which the nebula will begin to collapse. [2]
(ii) State one condition for the collapsed nebula in (c)(i) to form a star. [1]
(d) The mass of the Sun is $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg and the Sun will spend $8 \times 10^9$ years on the main sequence. The collapsed nebula in (c) also becomes a main sequence star. Estimate the time this star will spend on the main sequence. [3]
